issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
An had been a nurse for nearly twenty years, accustomed to the controlled chaos of a hospital ward. The real world, however, offered no such control. Six months ago, walking to his car after a late shift, that reality was driven home when a man stepped out from behind a pillar in the parking garage. The memory doesn't play like a film for An; it exists as a series of stark, silent snapshots. He sees the glint of a knife under the fluorescent lights, the man's wide, desperate eyes, and the rough texture of the concrete wall he was shoved against. The images are so clear, it’s as if he’s looking at photographs of the event in his mind, and when they surface, he often feels a phantom, searing pain in his right shoulder, exactly where he hit the wall.

In the weeks that followed, these photographic memories became the evidence for a harsh new verdict he had passed on himself. Replaying the silent images of his own frozen posture, he became convinced that there was something about him that had invited the attack, a weakness the mugger must have seen. This belief that he was intrinsically flawed began to curdle his view of everything else. The memory of his helplessness served as proof that nothing good could happen to him anymore; he had used up his share of luck. This sense of a bleak, foreclosed future meant his mind had nowhere to go but back to the trauma, keeping the memories sharp and readily accessible.

This deeply held belief that he was a magnet for disaster and that his future was empty has placed him in a state of constant, exhausting vigilance. An now feels a pervasive sense of threat that follows him from the moment he wakes. Sleep offers little escape, as he struggles to fall asleep and jerks awake at the slightest noise, his heart pounding. His conviction that he is fundamentally unsafe has recalibrated his entire nervous system. The world feels predatory, and his hopelessness deepens with every sleepless night, confirming his appraisal that things will never get better.

This ever-present sense of danger has forced him to adopt a rigid set of rules for survival. At work, he can no longer sit in the bustling breakroom unless he can find a chair in the corner, his back pressed firmly against a wall. The walk to his car is now a meticulous, ten-minute ordeal of scanning the environment, his head on a swivel, constantly checking behind him for footsteps that are never there. The hyperarousal fuels these behaviours, but it also makes him vulnerable; a sudden noise or a figure moving quickly in his periphery can instantly trigger the memory, bringing back the vivid pictures of the attack.

These strategies, meant to keep him safe, have become a cage. The very act of constantly checking his surroundings serves as a non-stop reminder of the trauma, ensuring the photographic memories are never far from the surface. He has started checking his reflection in shop windows and car mirrors, not out of vanity, but to see who might be behind him, a habit that leaves him feeling foolish and broken. This behaviour provides daily confirmation of his own defectiveness; he sees other people walking freely and is filled with a deep shame, which reinforces the belief that there is something intrinsically wrong with him. Convinced of his own vulnerability, he feels these routines are all that stand between him and another disaster, so he keeps his mind occupied at all times, a frantic mental distraction to keep the memories and the fear at bay.

The toll has been immense. His wife notes he seems distant, lost in his own world, his mind always busy. She has grown worried about the way he now checks every mirror in the car multiple times before pulling out of their driveway. The cycle of threat and avoidance has left him depleted, validating his hopeless belief that he has no future. He finally sought therapy after an intrusive memory struck him at the dinner table, causing him to cry out from the phantom pain in his shoulder, terrifying his wife and making him realize he could no longer manage this alone. He is exhausted by the vigilance, and beneath the fear, he quietly hopes to one day feel like the man he was before—competent, calm, and able to walk to his car without feeling like a target.
